edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De corona militis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Etenim, ut ipsam caussam coronae militaris aggrediar, puto prius conquirendum an in totum Christianis militia conveniat. Quale est alioquin de accidentibus retractare, cum a praecedentibus culpa sit? Credimusne humanum sacramentum divino superduci licere, et in alium dominum respondere post Christum? et ejerare patrem ac matrem, et omnem proximum, quos et lex honorari et post Deum diligi praecipit, quos et Evangelium solo Christo pluris non faciens, sic quoque honoravit? Licebit in gladio conversari, Domino pronuntiante, gladio periturum qui gladio fuerit usus? Et praelio operabitur filius pacis, cui nec litigare conveniet? Et vincula et carcerem et tormenta et supplicia administrabit, nec suarum ultor injuriarum? Jam stationes, aut alii magis faciet quam Christo? aut et Dominico die, quando nec Christo? et excubabit pro templis, quibus renuntiavit? et coenabit illic ubi apostolo non placet? et quos interdiu exorcismis fugavit, noctibus defensabit, incumbens et requiescens super pilum quo perfossum est latus Christi? vexillum quoque portabit aemulum Christi? et signum postulabit a principe, qui jam a Deo accepit? mortuus etiam tuba inquietabitur aeneatoris, qui excitari a tuba angeli exspectat? et cremabitur ex disciplina castrensi Christianus, cui cremare non licuit, cui Christus merita ignis indulsit? Quanta alia in delictis circumspici possunt castrensium munium, transgression interpretanda? Ipsum de castris lucis in castra tenebrarum nomen deferre, transgressio est. Plane, si quos militia praeventos fides posterior invenit, alia conditio est, ut illorum quos Joannes admittebat ad lavacrum, ut centurionum fidelissimorum, quem Christus probat, et quem Petrus catechizat: dum tamen, suscepta fide atque signata, aut deserendum statim sit, ut a multis actum, aut omnibus modis cavillandum, ne quid adversus Deum committatur, quae nec ex militia permittuntur; aut novissime perpetiendum pro Deo, quod aeque fides pagana condixit. Nec enim delictorum impunitatem, aut martyriorum immunitatem militia promittet. Nusquam Christianus aliud est. Unum Evangelium, et idem Jesus, negaturus omnem negatorem, et confessurus omnem confessorem Dei, et salvam facturus animam pro nomine ejus amissam, perditurus autem de contrario adversus nomen ejus lucri habitam. Apud hunc tam miles est paganus fidelis, quam paganus est miles infidelis. Non admittit status fidei necessitates. Nulla est necessitas delinquendi, quibus una est necessitas non delinquendi. Nam et ad sacrificandum et directo negandum necessitate quis premitur tormentorum sive poenarum: tamen nec illi necessitati disciplina connivet, quia potior est necessitas timendae negationis et obeundi martyrii, quam evadendae passionis et implendi officii. Caeterum subvertit totam substantiam sacramenti causatio ejusmodi, ut etiam voluntariis delictis fibulam laxet. Nam et voluntas poterit necessitas contendi, habens scilicet unde cogatur. Vel ipsam praestruxerim et ad caeteras officialium coronarum caussas, quibus familiarissima est advocatio necessitatis: cum idcirco aut officia fugienda sint, ne in delictis incidamus; aut et martyria toleranda sint, ut officia rumpamus. De prima specie quaestionis etiam militiae ipsius illicitae, plura non faciam, ut secunda reddatur, ne si omni ope expulero militiam, frustra jam de corona militari provocarim.
pass_a_gloss: For, so that I may approach the very cause of the military crown, I think it must first be investigated whether military service is suitable for Christians in general. What is the point of discussing accidents, when the fault lies in what has gone before? Do we believe it is permissible for a human oath to be placed above a divine one, and to respond to another lord after Christ? And to forsake father and mother, and every neighbor, whom both the law commands to be honored and, after God, to be loved, whom the Gospel also honored, not making them more valuable than Christ alone? Will it be permissible to engage in sword fighting, when the Lord says that whoever uses the sword will perish by the sword? And will the son of peace work in battle, when it is not fitting for him even to quarrel? And will he administer chains and prison and torments and punishments, without avenging his own injuries? Now, will he do guard duty, or will he do more than Christ did? Or will he even do it on the Lord's day, when not even Christ did? And will he keep watch over temples, which he has renounced? And will he dine where it does not please the apostle? And will he defend at night those whom he has put to flight with exorcisms during the day, leaning and resting on the spear with which Christ's side was pierced? Will he also carry a standard rivaling Christ? And will he demand a sign from a commander, when he has already received it from God? Even when dead, will the trumpet of the bugler disturb him, when he expects to be awakened by the trumpet of an angel? And will a Christian be burned according to military discipline, when it was not permissible for him to burn, and when Christ has granted him the merits of fire? How many other transgressions of military duties can be seen, which must be interpreted as faults? To transfer one's name from the camp of light to the camp of darkness is itself a transgression. Certainly, if faith later finds some people who have been prevented from serving in the military, their situation is different, as with those whom John admitted to baptism, such as the most faithful centurions, whom Christ approves and whom Peter instructs: yet, once they have accepted the faith and been sealed, either they must immediately desert, as many have done, or they must find a way to avoid everything that is against God, which is not permitted by military service; or, finally, they must endure everything for God, which pagan faith has also granted. For military service does not promise impunity for faults or immunity from martyrdom. Nowhere is a Christian anything else. There is one Gospel, and the same Jesus, who denies every denier and confesses every confessor of God, and who will save the soul that has been lost for his name, but will destroy the one who has gained the world against his name. In his eyes, a faithful pagan soldier is the same as an unfaithful pagan soldier. Faith does not admit the necessities of status. There is no necessity to sin, when there is one necessity not to sin. For even when someone is forced by necessity to sacrifice or to deny directly, whether by torments or punishments, yet discipline does not yield to that necessity, because the necessity of fearing denial and undergoing martyrdom is greater than the necessity of avoiding passion and fulfilling duty. Besides, this kind of justification subverts the entire substance of the sacrament, so that it even loosens the bond for voluntary faults. For the will can also be a necessity, having, of course, something that can compel it. Or I may have already established this, and also the other causes of official crowns, to which the advocacy of necessity is very familiar: since either the offices must be avoided, lest we fall into faults, or martyrdoms must be tolerated, so that we may break with offices. I will not say more about the first part of the question, which is about the illegitimacy of military service itself, so that the second part may be addressed, lest, if I expel military service with all my might, I may in vain provoke discussion about the military crown.

to refer to the Christian community

pass_b_english: I start with the whole question because I want to get at the real issue: is military service even compatible with being a Christian? It makes no sense to debate the details when the root is rotten. Do we really think a human oath can override a divine one, or that we can pledge allegiance to another lord after Christ? Do we abandon father, mother, and every neighbor the Law commands us to honor and love after God—people the Gospel also honored, without putting them above Christ alone? Can we live by the sword when the Lord says whoever uses the sword will perish by the sword (Matthew 26:52)? Can a son of peace take part in battle when it does not even become him to quarrel? Will he inflict chains, prison, torture, and execution without avenging his own wrongs? Will he pull guard duty, or do more than Christ did? Will he do it on the Lord's Day when not even Christ did? Will he stand watch over temples he has renounced? Will he eat where the apostle says not to? Will he defend at night the very spirits he exorcised by day, leaning on the spear that pierced Christ's side? Will he carry a standard that rivals Christ's? Will he demand a sign from a commander when he has already received one from God? Even dead, will a bugler's trumpet disturb him when he waits for the angel's trumpet? Will a Christian be burned by military discipline when burning was forbidden him and Christ granted him the merit of fire? How many other violations of military duty must be counted as sins? Simply moving your name from the camp of light to the camp of darkness is itself a sin.

If faith finds a man already in the ranks, his case is different—like the centurions John baptized, whom Christ approved and Peter instructed. But once they have accepted the faith and been sealed, they must either desert immediately, as many did, or find every possible way to avoid anything that opposes God, since military service does not allow it; or, finally, they must endure everything for God, which even pagan faith permits. Military service promises neither impunity for sins nor immunity from martyrdom. A Christian is a Christian everywhere. There is one Gospel, one Jesus, who denies every denier and confesses every confessor of God, who saves the soul lost for his name and destroys the one who gained the world against his name. In his eyes a faithful pagan soldier is no different from an unfaithful pagan soldier. The demands of faith admit no exemptions based on rank. There is no necessity to sin when the only necessity is not to sin. Even when someone is forced by torture or punishment to sacrifice or deny directly, discipline does not yield to that pressure, because the necessity of refusing to deny and accepting martyrdom outweighs the necessity of avoiding suffering and doing one's duty. Moreover, this kind of justification guts the whole substance of the sacrament, loosening the bond even for voluntary sins. Will can masquerade as necessity when it has something to gain. I have already established this for the other official crowns where the plea of necessity is commonplace: either the offices must be avoided so we do not fall into sin, or martyrdoms must be endured so we can break with those offices. I will not press the first part of the question—the illegitimacy of military service itself—any further, so the second part can be addressed; otherwise, if I drive out military service entirely, I will have raised the issue of the military crown in vain.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation. Pass B provides a fluent rendering that includes the required scripture identification for the allusion to Matthew 26:52 (gladio periturum qui gladio fuerit usus). All theological distinctions regarding necessity and the nature of the sacrament are preserved.
